**This is a video lecture.** It is released on **9 November 2026** and has *no*
on-site session on a Monday — you work through it on your own, at your own pace.
It is recorded as eight videos (about 110 minutes in total).
Please post any questions in the
[Moodle forum](https://elearning.uni-flensburg.de/moodle/course/view.php?id=17920);
we also take them up in the concluding Q&A session of 11 December.

**Take-home examination II** on literature reviews belongs to this lecture. It
is published on Moodle on **10 November 2026** and must be submitted there by
**22 November 2026, 23:59** — so make sure you have worked through the video
before you start on it.

## 🎯 Content and goals

The lecture uses the systematic literature review as the reference model and
shows what it means for the literature review section of your term paper or
thesis. After this session you can …

1. **choose** a review type that fits the purpose;
2. **explain** what a review can and cannot establish;
3. **translate** a topic into a concept table and a search string;
4. **assess** a search: precision, recall, validation;
5. **select** studies by explicit criteria and document this in a **PRISMA**
   flow diagram;
6. **synthesize** with a concept matrix;
7. **identify** biases — in literature, databases, search and synthesis.

Everything in the lecture and the tutorial works with **open tools only**: the
search uses [OpenAlex](https://openalex.org), a free and open database. Its
main limitation — many records without abstracts — is taught explicitly,
together with ways to compensate for it.

The running example is the literature on **capabilities and routines** — from
Nelson and Winter's evolutionary theory to dynamic capabilities in strategic
management. Shorter examples come from firm growth, path dependence, and the
debate on corporate social and financial performance.

## 🧰 Tutorial and templates

- [**A mini systematic review in eight steps**](lit-review-tutorial/index.qmd) —
  the hands-on companion to the lecture. It walks you through a complete small
  review in OpenAlex, from the concept table to the flow diagram, including how
  to fill in missing abstracts. A digression adds a second database —
  [EconBiz](https://www.econbiz.de), the free subject portal for economics,
  or Web of Science — and an optional R part runs the whole search from R,
  including the EconBiz API.

- [**RM-LitReviewTutorial**](https://github.com/graebnerc/RM-LitReviewTutorial) — the tutorial's example review as a
  complete, reproducible R project on GitHub: one Quarto report with all
  code, all saved search results and the flow diagram.

- [**Workbook with all templates**](lit-review-tutorial/L08-review-templates.xlsx)
  (download) — a **search log**, a **screening sheet**, a **concept matrix**
  and a sheet for **limitations**, which you can reuse for your term paper. It
  works in Excel, LibreOffice and Numbers.

- [**AI disclosure**](ai-disclosure/index.qmd) — the template for declaring any
  use of AI tools in your review, whether in a term paper, a thesis or the
  take-home.

OpenAlex is free; you only need a free account (and API key) for the R part.
EconBiz is free and needs no account at all.
For the optional Web of Science digression, access is provided through the
university library; see the
[ZHB database entry](https://dbis.ur.de/HDFL/resources/3366?lang=de).

## 📚 Mandatory Reading

- @snyder2019literature — a short overview of review types and how to choose
  between them, written for business research.
- @page2021prisma — the PRISMA 2020 statement. Concentrate on the checklist and
  the flow diagram; the rest you can skim.

## 🏆 Further Readings

*On method:*

- @tranfield2003towards — the classic argument for systematic reviews in
  management, and why they need to differ from the medical template.
- @webster2002analyzing — the origin of the concept matrix.
- @grant2009typology — fourteen review types, if you want the full map.
- @page2021prismaexplanation — the PRISMA explanation and elaboration paper;
  use it as a reference, not as reading.
- @rethlefsen2021prismas — PRISMA-S, on how to report the search itself.
- @gusenbauer2020which — which search systems are suitable for systematic
  reviews (and why Google Scholar is not one of them).

*On OpenAlex and the political economy of research information:*

- @priem2022openalex — what OpenAlex is and how it was built.
- @zbw2026econbiz — the subject portal for economics and business studies,
  strong on books, working papers and German-language literature.
- @stansfield2025analyzing — a test of OpenAlex for a real systematic review.
- @borrego2025openalex — features and limitations, including missing
  abstracts.
- @lariviere2015oligopoly — the concentration of academic publishing.
- The [Barcelona Declaration on Open Research Information](https://barcelona-declaration.org).
- The official [PRISMA website](https://www.prisma-statement.org/) with
  checklists and flow-diagram templates.

*Reviews used as examples in the lecture:*

- @becker2004organizational and @lane2006reification — two reviews that show
  how a concept drifts as a literature grows.
- @schilke2018quo — a content-analytic review of dynamic capabilities.

*Two systematic reviews I was involved in:* @aistleitner2021capability and
@graebner2023degrowth.

*Take-home examination II (pass/fail; you must pass two of the three take-home
examinations to be admitted to the final exam — see the
[seminar description](/content/SeminarDescription.qmd)):*

- Conduct a small systematic literature review on a question that will be given
  to you. The task is published on
  [Moodle](https://elearning.uni-flensburg.de/moodle/course/view.php?id=17920)
  on 10 November 2026 (due 22 November, 23:59) and follows the steps of the
  [tutorial](lit-review-tutorial/index.qmd). Do not forget the
  [AI disclosure](ai-disclosure/index.qmd).

*Suggested exercise (not graded):*

- Take the literature review section of a paper you have recently read and fill
  in a concept matrix for the studies it cites. Is the section a synthesis, or a
  sequence of summaries?
